title: RPO / RTO
subtitle: Measuring maximum data loss (RPO) and downtime (RTO) against real infrastructure cost curves.
keyTakeaways: RPO (Recovery Point Objective) measures how much data you can afford to lose in seconds or hours; RTO (Recovery Time Objective) measures how long you can tolerate being offline before service is restored.
RPO is determined by data replication pipelines (synchronous replication, streaming WAL, or periodic snapshots); RTO is determined by automation, compute warmth, and traffic failover speed.
Targeting zero RPO and zero RTO across regions multiplies infrastructure and maintenance costs; tier your microservices by business impact rather than treating all endpoints equally.

sections.heading: Defining RPO and RTO in Operational Terms
sections.body: RPO and RTO are the foundational metrics of disaster recovery planning. While often grouped together, they measure two completely different operational trade-offs and are driven by different technical mechanisms.
bullets: RPO (Recovery Point Objective) looks backward in time: If a database crashes at 14:00 and you restore from a 13:00 backup, you have lost 1 hour of transactions—your RPO is 1 hour. Achieving an RPO of seconds requires continuous streaming Write-Ahead Logs (WAL) or synchronous replication.

RTO (Recovery Time Objective) looks forward in time: If a service fails at 14:00 and traffic is restored at 14:30, your downtime is 30 minutes—your RTO is 30 minutes. RTO includes failure detection time, standby instance boot time, health check validation, and DNS/routing updates.
The RPO/RTO equation: Total downtime (RTO) = Time to detect failure + Time to promote database standby + Time to scale application compute + Time to shift user traffic.

sections.heading: The Cost Curve of Near-Zero RPO and Service Tiering
sections.body: Aiming for RPO = 0 and RTO = 0 for every microservice is one of the quickest ways to inflate infrastructure budgets. As recovery objectives approach zero, the required engineering architecture shifts from simple automated backups to complex multi-region active-active deployments.
bullets: The exponential cost curve: Moving from a 24-hour backup (RTO: 4h, RPO: 24h) to a Pilot Light setup (RTO: 30m, RPO: <1m) increases storage and replication costs modestly. Moving from Pilot Light to Warm Standby doubles compute costs. Moving to Active-Active (RTO: ~0, RPO: ~0) triples infrastructure spend and introduces complex conflict resolution logic.

Service tiering by business criticality: Categorize services into tiers. Tier 0 (Payment processing, Auth) gets Warm Standby or Active-Active with RTO < 5m and RPO < 1s. Tier 1 (Order history, Search) gets Pilot Light with RTO < 30m. Tier 2 (Internal analytics, PDF invoice generation) gets Backup & Restore with RTO < 4h and RPO < 24h.

Validating RTO assumptions: Never trust an untested RTO target. If a team claims an RTO of 15 minutes but has never practiced rebuilding their Kubernetes cluster from scratch in a secondary region, real recovery during a crisis will take hours.

tradeOffs.pros: Guarantees zero committed transactions are lost even if an entire facility or zone is destroyed.
tradeOffs.cons: Every write pays the network latency to the replica; replica network hiccups directly stall write throughput on the primary.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Core payment ledgers, banking accounts, and regulatory compliance records.

tradeOffs.pros: Sub-millisecond local write latency; primary continues processing writes even during temporary network jitter to the replica.
tradeOffs.cons: A crash of the primary can lose up to a few seconds of committed transactions, requiring post-incident reconciliation.
tradeOffs.bestFor: High-scale consumer web applications, social feeds, product catalogs, and SaaS platforms.

interviewTip: Clarify RPO and RTO within the first three minutes of any system design interview involving storage or disaster recovery: ask whether the system requires RPO = 0 (synchronous replication) or if an RPO of under 5 seconds with asynchronous streaming is acceptable. That single answer dictates the entire database architecture.
